title: White Dwarfs
objective: After this level you can describe white dwarfs and why they slowly cool.
summary: A white dwarf is a dead star’s core: Earth-sized, nearly Sun-massive, so dense a teaspoon weighs tons, and slowly cooling.

cards.headline: A teaspoon of this star would weigh several tons.
cards.body: When the planetary nebula from Level 67 drifts away, something is left behind. It’s small, it’s hot, and it’s astonishingly heavy for its size.

cards.headline: A star-sized core in an Earth-sized ball
cards.body: What’s left is the star’s exposed core: a white dwarf. It’s about the size of Earth, but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s. Picture roughly a star’s worth of matter packed into a ball the size of our planet. The result is absurdly dense: a teaspoonful would weigh several tons on Earth. Your kitchen scale would not survive the experiment.

cards.headline: Slowly fading
cards.body: A white dwarf no longer fuses anything. It shines only with leftover heat, like an oven after it’s switched off, and slowly cools over billions of years. That’s why it sits in the lower left of the H–R diagram: hot, but dim. A famous example is Sirius B, the faint partner of Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It’s also the most common ending: most stars in the Milky Way, the Sun included, will finish as white dwarfs.

cards.headline: White dwarfs: understood
learned: A white dwarf is a dead Sun-like star’s core
It’s about Earth-sized with much of the Sun’s mass
A teaspoon would weigh several tons
It no longer fuses; it slowly cools

questions.prompt: How big is a typical white dwarf?

options.label: About the size of the Sun
About the size of a city
options.rationale: That’s closer to a neutron star.

questions.explanation: A white dwarf packs a mass comparable to the Sun’s into a ball about the size of Earth.

questions.prompt: Why does a white dwarf slowly get dimmer?

options.label: It no longer fuses, so it just cools off
It is pulled apart by nearby planets
Its fusion slowly speeds up
options.rationale: It no longer fuses at all.

questions.explanation: With no fusion left, a white dwarf only radiates stored heat, slowly cooling over billions of years.

questions.prompt: From Level 9: why will the Sun end as a white dwarf instead of a supernova?

options.label: It isn’t massive enough to explode
It has already used up all its helium
options.rationale: Mass decides the ending, not helium.

options.label: Its planets will absorb the explosion
options.rationale: Planets play no part in a star’s ending.

options.label: White dwarfs only form near other stars
options.rationale: Most stars end as white dwarfs on their own.

questions.explanation: Only stars much more massive than the Sun explode as supernovae, so the Sun fades out as a white dwarf.
